_comment: Canonical-claim manifest for check-claims.js (#300). Each entry pins a rule that MUST keep being stated by every file listed, because #294 proved that a correct claim fixed in one file routinely goes stale, narrowed or absent in the others. Read check-claims.js's header before trusting a green run: this guard confirms a claim TRAVELLED, never that it is TRUE, and it cannot see a fix that says more than intended. Patterns are JS regex sources matched case-insensitively against the file with whitespace collapsed and markdown emphasis markers stripped, so one entry spans the wording variants a claim legitimately has. Consumer lists were derived by measuring the current tree, not by assumption — the issue that proposed this guard listed phrases that did not exist verbatim anywhere.
_negators_comment: The ONE definition of a negation word, expanded into every pattern's {{NEG}} placeholder by check-claims.js. Round 7 exists because round 6 claimed to have unified two copies and instead wrote the same alternation twice: deleting `avoid` from only the lookbehind copy left every declared case passing while `avoid read the comments and the review threads` was accepted. Two literals are not one definition no matter what the commit message says. The guard also DERIVES a rejection case for each negator in BOTH positions from this string, so the tests cannot drift from it either -- there is no hand-written list to forget. Apostrophe forms are here because the normalizer deliberately does not strip apostrophes (that would corrupt ordinary prose), so `don't arm a check-in` needs the contraction spelled out.
_negatorFloor_comment: The definition-independent BASELINE. Round 7 claimed literal cases cover what derived probes cannot -- narrowing the definition -- and then pinned only the four negators review had happened to find. Round 8 deleted `ignores` and the guard stayed green, which is the same carry-it-to-the-siblings defect for the fourth time in this PR: the mechanism was identified correctly and applied to a subset. This list is checked BEHAVIOURALLY -- every entry must still be rejected in every declared position -- so it does not drift into being a second copy of `negators` that agrees by luck. Removing a value from `negators` now fails here, which is exactly the edit derivation cannot see. Adding one to `negators` without adding it here is fine and deliberate: the floor is a MINIMUM, not a mirror.

claims.why: A clean Codex rerun can arrive as a 👍 reaction or as an INLINE REVIEW-THREAD REPLY, and an inline reply never enters the comment list. A file that says only 'check the comments' sends a session to a gate it cannot clear. Round 35 of #294 found the narrowed form in nine files while the source said both. The pattern requires a positive lookup VERB because the nouns alone certified the exact inversion — 'ignore the PR's comments and its review threads' — and the negator lookbehind is there because 'do not read' supplied the verb while reversing the instruction. Both alternations are \b-anchored after an unanchored 'read' was found matching the tail of 'review-thread', letting an already-inverted sentence supply its own verb. Round 5 closed a subtler inversion than round 4's: requiring a positive verb is not enough if the gap between it and the channels can hold a NEGATIVE one. 'check the PR status, but ignore its comments AND its review threads' satisfied a bare gap, because 'check' supplied the verb while 'ignore' governed the nouns. The gap is now a tempered token admitting no negation word, so the verb it requires is the verb that actually governs. Round 6 found the same defect one level down and it is the most instructive instance: the fix itself introduced a SECOND negator list. The lookbehind already rejected never/not/dont/avoid/skip; the tempered gap I added rejected a different, overlapping set, so 'but avoid its comments AND its review threads' passed while 'but ignore ...' failed. Two lists expressing one idea drift silently. There is now one alternation used in both positions, and mustNotMatch carries a case per negator so the SUITE is what keeps them synchronised rather than a maintainer's memory. Round 7: round 6 said 'one alternation used in both positions' and wrote the string TWICE. Codex deleted `avoid` from a single copy and every declared case still passed. The alternation now lives once, at the manifest's top level, expanded into {{NEG}}; the guard also DERIVES a rejection case per negator per position from it, so the tests cannot drift from the definition either. The explicit cases below anchor the specific negators review paid to find -- derived probes catch DRIFT between positions, but narrowing the definition would delete a negator and its probe together, and only a literal case catches that.
mustNotMatch: ignore the PR's comments and its review threads
do not read the comments and the review threads
as an inline review-thread reply — so ignore the comments AND the review threads
check the PR's comments
read the review threads
check the PR status, but ignore its comments AND its review threads
read the run log, then disregard the comments and the review threads
check the label; never look for the comments and its review threads
check the PR status, but avoid its comments AND its review threads
check the PR status, but dont check its comments AND its review threads
check the label, then skip the comments AND the review threads
check the run, without reading the comments AND its review threads
avoid read the comments and the review threads
don't read the comments and the review threads
check the PR status, but don't check its comments AND its review threads

negatorProbe.lookbehind: %s read the comments and the review threads
negatorProbe.gap: check the PR status, but %s its comments and its review threads

claims.why: Codex-authored and naming the current head proves the run happened, not that it was clean — a review WITH live findings names the head too. Round 36 of #294 fixed the inverted form, which had authorised merging over open findings. Two drafts of this entry were wrong in opposite directions and both are instructive: the first accepted 'a reaction is not a verdict' — a DIFFERENT rule, about attribution — and so certified a consumer that never stated this claim; the second over-corrected to a pattern so narrow it could not see automations.md's 'establishes a RESPONSE, not a verdict', and declared the claim source-only on that basis. A pattern that matches a neighbouring rule reports coverage that does not exist; a pattern that misses a real carrier hides a consumer that can drift.
claims.pattern: \bresponse\b[^.]{0,30}?(?:is not a verdict|, not a verdict)

consumers.why: Found by review, NOT by --derive, and the reason is the entry's own recorded limit made concrete: this carrier states the claim ANAPHORICALLY — 'a clean current-head Codex verdict — a response naming the head is not one, since a review with live findings names it too'. The claim-level pattern needs the words 'is not a verdict' adjacent to 'response'; here the predicate is the pronoun 'one', pointing back to 'verdict' a clause earlier. No widening of the claim-level pattern reaches that without also matching sentences that are not this claim, which is why it gets its own pattern instead. This is the repo's PRIMARY instruction file and the merge gate it describes is the one that authorises merging over live findings, so it is the last carrier that should have been unlisted.
consumers.pattern: response naming the head is not one
mustNotMatch: a response naming the head is one
a response naming the head is a clean verdict
a Codex response is not a verdict
a reaction is not a verdict you can attribute
consumers.whyMustNotMatch: The first two are this override's own inversion: a carrier that flipped 'is not one' to 'is one' states the OPPOSITE rule and must not certify. The third is the case that proves these cases exercise the OVERRIDE rather than the claim pattern -- the claim-level regex MATCHES it, this override rejects it, so it can only pass by the override doing work. Round 6 caught the absence of exactly that: every case here was a copied wait-gate string, rejected by both patterns, proving nothing. The fourth pins the neighbouring-rule confusion this entry already made once.

mustNotMatch: a reaction is not a verdict you can attribute
a response naming the head is a clean verdict
a Codex response is a verdict

claims.why: The companion entry `unreachable-review-terminal-states` pins the SENTENCE 'The two states are …' at each consumer. Codex, #336 round 9: that catches a consumer drifting away from the sentence and NOT a third bullet appended to the list in git.md, after which every consumer keeps asserting 'the two states' truthfully-as-written while the source admits three. check-claims.js's own header names this as one of its three documented blind spots -- it 'cannot see a fix that says MORE than intended' (rounds 38-39 of #294) -- so closing it needs a pattern about STRUCTURE, not wording. This one requires the summary sentence to follow the outage bullet with NO further bullet between them: append a third and the tempered gap rejects it, so the source and its summary cannot disagree about how many states there are. sourceOnly because the structure exists only in git.md; the consumers carry the sentence, which the companion entry pins. ⚠️ What it does NOT catch: a bullet inserted BEFORE the unavailable one, or a state added somewhere other than this list. The realistic edit is an append, which is what this covers.
claims.pattern: outage — the request could not be made or accepted at all(?:(?!- )[^])*?The two states are
mustNotMatch: outage — the request could not be made or accepted at all: the App is not installed. - **stale head** — Codex cannot reach it. The two states are
The two states are an unavailable reply still inside its reset window
outage — the request could not be made or accepted at all

claims.why: `unreachable-review-test-name` pins the test's NAME and says in its own rationale that it cannot see the CONTENT; #336 round 7 then proved that by finding five files that named the test while stating the opposite rule around it. This entry is the other half, and Codex asked for it by naming the drift it would permit: widen the canonical test so an accepted-but-silent request counts as an outage, or drop the reset bound so a stale usage-limit reply stays valid forever, and every merge consumer -- all of which admit 'any state that test admits' -- would authorise removing the blocker and merging while a review is still obtainable or in flight. The name-only pattern passes unchanged through both. So the two states are stated in one canonical sentence at each consumer and pinned whole: an *unavailable* reply STILL INSIDE ITS RESET WINDOW, a request that COULD NOT BE MADE OR ACCEPTED at all, and NEVER ELAPSED SILENCE. All three fragments are required and in order, because each was a separate defect on this PR -- round 4 deleted a 30-minute timer that made silence sufficient, round 4 also found the unavailable reply had no expiry, and round 6 found a third statement of outage still defined as 'produced no signal'. A pattern requiring only two of the three would certify the third's regression.
claims.pattern: still inside its reset window(?:(?!\b(?:{{NEG}})\b)[^.]){0,60}?could not be made or accepted(?:(?!\b(?:{{NEG}})\b)[^.]){0,40}?never elapsed silence
mustNotMatch: an unavailable reply still inside its reset window, or a request that could not be made or accepted at all
a request that could not be made or accepted at all — never elapsed silence
an unavailable reply, or a request that could not be made or accepted at all — never elapsed silence
still inside its reset window, or a request that could not be made or accepted, but never mind elapsed silence

negatorProbe.gap: still inside its reset window, %s could not be made or accepted at all — never elapsed silence

claims.why: #336 round 5 made every reaction-only round escalate to the owner. Round 6 showed that is wrong for the common case: when a PR's FIRST Codex pass comes back clean as a reaction, codex-monitor never adds `codex-flagged` at all, so the reaction ladder clears the verdict gate, the absent label satisfies the label gate, and the merge proceeds unattended. I scoped the rule, the gate framing and the readiness agent -- and round 7 found the unconditional version still standing in the auto-merge gate, CLAUDE.md, automations.md and cicd-setup.md, where a session would have spent a metered review request or involved the owner for nothing. Seventh round of one rule stated in several places and only some updated, and the FIRST one to survive after `unreachable-review-test-name` was added -- which is the evidence that pinning the test's NAME does not pin its CONTENT, exactly as that entry says. Codex asked for this entry by name for that reason. ⚠️ What this pins is the POSITIVE path: a session that drops the no-label carve-out and reverts to escalating unconditionally fails here. It does not pin the negative half (that a label which IS present escalates) -- that half is the conservative direction, and a carrier that over-escalates wastes a request rather than merging past a review. Consumers derived by measuring the tree, not assumed. The pattern requires the LADDER PREREQUISITE between the two halves, because without it the regex also accepted 'Where no codex-flagged label is present, the merge proceeds' -- which turns absence of an asynchronously-written label into sufficient merge evidence, the exact opposite of the surrounding rule that its absence proves nothing. A guard that accepts the dangerous shortening of the claim it pins is worse than no guard, since it reports the regression as coverage; that shortened form is in mustNotMatch. It also requires the word UNATTENDED, because the pattern ended at 'merge proceeds' and an owner-gated suffix -- 'the merge proceeds only after escalating to the owner', 'after owner approval' -- satisfied it while reinstating the escalation this claim exists to prevent. A pattern that stops before the consequence pins the condition and not the outcome. The READINESS AGENT is deliberately NOT a consumer: it cannot run the ladder and round 8 taught it that the no-label merge result is the merger's conclusion, so requiring it to restate that conclusion would force it to keep the shadow copy that went stale in rounds 5, 6 and 8. It states the part that IS its own -- an absent label removes only the label blocker -- and nothing further.
claims.pattern: no codex-flagged label is present(?:(?!\b(?:{{NEG}})\b)[^.]){0,40}?ladder is the whole gate(?:(?!\b(?:{{NEG}})\b)[^.]){0,40}?merge proceeds unattended
mustNotMatch: a codex-flagged label is present, so the merge proceeds
no codex-flagged label is present, but never let the merge proceeds
no codex-flagged label is present
the ladder is the whole gate and the merge proceeds
no codex-flagged label is present, so escalate; instead the merge proceeds
Where no codex-flagged label is present, the merge proceeds
no codex-flagged label is present, and the ladder is the whole gate
no codex-flagged label is present, the ladder is the whole gate and the merge proceeds only after escalating to the owner
no codex-flagged label is present, the ladder is the whole gate and the merge proceeds after owner approval

negatorProbe.gap: no codex-flagged label is present, but %s the merge proceeds

claims.why: #336 defined the *unreachable-review test* -- the one condition under which a session may take `codex-flagged` off by hand -- and then spent three consecutive review rounds being shown a consumer that had dropped it. Round 4: the commit that INTRODUCED the name coined two aliases for it in the same breath ('last-resort test', 'recorded-evidence test') across five files, which is the shadow-copy mechanism the name was introduced to remove, reproduced inside its own fix. Round 5: the test's defining sentence still permitted silence. Round 6: a third statement of its outage exit survived at the verdict gate. Each time I claimed propagation and each time a reader found a copy I had not searched for. This repo's established answer to that class is a checker, not vigilance, and the name is exactly what makes the search runnable -- so the search runs in CI now. ⚠️ WHAT THIS PINS, stated plainly because the guard's header demands it: this pins the NAME, not the substance. A consumer that says 'unreachable-review test' while describing it wrongly passes; the three drifts above were all of that kind ONCE the name was present, which is why the name went in. What it catches is the failure that actually recurred first -- a consumer that stops naming the test and starts re-describing it, because a description cannot be searched for and the next revision will miss it. Consumers were derived by measuring the tree at 0ee2527, not assumed. The lookbehind admits an ARTICLE between the negator and the name, which the other entries' do not need: every pointer here reads 'where the unreachable-review test admits it', so a bare word-before-phrase lookbehind checks 'the' and lets 'never the unreachable-review test admits it' through. The guard's own derived probes caught that on the first run of this entry -- which is the entry justifying itself: a mechanism found the drift I would have shipped.
mustNotMatch: the last-resort test admits it
bounds by a recorded-evidence test
never the unreachable-review test
a test for unreachable review

claims.why: ci-notify resolves ONE open PR from a head SHA, else branch plus head-repo owner. The WEAK failure (no unique candidate, so it exits silently) is not the dangerous one and is stated separately in every carrier; the dangerous one is that even a UNIQUE match proves nothing, because a repository_dispatch run carries the DEFAULT-BRANCH SHA and can uniquely match an unrelated promotion PR, which then receives the comment. The pattern deliberately requires the unique-match wording: an earlier draft matched only 'not a guaranteed wake', which is the weak sentence, so deleting the entire unique-match warning would have left this guard green. The lookbehind is the second half of the same lesson: 'unique' unanchored is a SUBSTRING of 'non-unique', so a carrier that regressed to warning about NON-unique matches — the weak case again, now wearing the strong case's words — satisfied the tightened pattern too. Requiring no word character or hyphen before it is what makes the tightening real.
mustNotMatch: a non-unique match is not proof of coverage
a green run is not a guaranteed wake
a unique match is proof of coverage

claims.why: The counterpart to the wake gap above: when a run could end without waking the session, the check-in is what keeps the PR from being abandoned mid-flight. Rounds 37 and 39 of #294 were both this claim failing to reach a consumer — round 39's was in plugins/directives-toolkit/scripts/wait-gate.sh, whose PreToolUse message is the highest-authority copy of the rule because it is delivered unprompted at the decision point, and every .md-only sweep missed it. That carrier is listed here, and the pattern accepts 'arm a check-in' / 'arms a check-in' as well as 'arm the check-in' because the shell copy uses the indefinite article — an entry that named the round-39 file in its rationale while omitting it from its consumers, as the first draft of this one did, reproduces the exact failure it cites. The leading word boundary matters more here than in most patterns because this claim's exact INVERSION contains it: 'disarm a check-in' is the opposite instruction and the unanchored form certified it. A pattern that accepts the negation of its own claim is worse than no pattern, since it reports the regression as coverage — so the boundary is required in the per-consumer variant below as well. The negator lookbehind rejects 'never arm a check-in'. It deliberately checks only the word IMMEDIATELY before the verb: a clause-level negation scan was designed, measured and rejected, because ci-notify.yml legitimately reads 'a green run is not a guaranteed wake and a waiting session still arms a check-in', where the negator belongs to a different proposition in the same clause. 'never explicitly arm a check-in' therefore still passes; narrowing that needs the claim's CONDITION pinned, not just its verb. Round 7 added the apostrophe forms: the normalizer deliberately does not strip apostrophes -- doing so would corrupt ordinary prose -- so `dont` in the negator list did not cover `don't arm a check-in`, the way a person actually writes the inversion.

consumers.why: This file states the rule TWICE — once in its explanatory header comment, once inside the echo the PreToolUse hook actually delivers. The claim-level pattern matched the header, so deleting the instruction from the DELIVERED message left the guard green on the copy that carries the most authority (it reaches a session unprompted, at the decision point). The pattern below requires the delivered message's own opening text, so only the emitted form satisfies it.
mustNotMatch: BLOCKED by directives wait-gate: do not background a `sleep` to wait. Instead: (1) for CI / PR / deploy outcomes, let the event wake the session (PR + CI webhooks) - and DISARM A CHECK-IN ALONGSIDE IT, not instead of it; (2) that check-in is `send_later`.

BLOCKED by directives wait-gate: do not background a `sleep` to wait. Instead: (1) for CI / PR / deploy outcomes, let the event wake the session (PR + CI webhooks); (2) use `send_later` (the pre-approved primary).
# The hook arms a check-in alongside it, but the delivered message below says nothing about one.
consumers.whyMustNotMatch: An override exists to be STRICTER than the claim pattern, so it needs its own inversions or the escape hatch reopens every defect the claim-level suite closed. Codex reproduced exactly that: widen this override back to an unbounded arms?, invert the delivered message to DISARM, and every claim-level case still passed while this strict consumer reported OK. The third case is the original round-2 defect restated - the file's HEADER COMMENT satisfying the pattern while the DELIVERED echo has lost the instruction - so the override must reject it even though it plainly states the rule. The third case is also the override-exercising one: the claim-level pattern MATCHES it (it plainly says 'arms a check-in') while this override rejects it for lacking the delivered message's own opening text -- so it can only pass by the override doing work, which is the property the guard now requires of every override suite.

mustNotMatch: disarm a check-in
never arm a check-in whenever the run's SHA is not your PR's head
do not arm the check-in
dont arm a check-in
the harness disarms a check-in for you
don't arm a check-in
doesn't arm a check-in
